content: 1. A study conducted in Brazil explored the use of specific tools for cervical lesion screening in women living with HIV. The findings were published in the Brazilian Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2018, highlighting the importance of tailored screening approaches for this population. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Debeaudrap et al. in 2019 examined the rates of residual or recurrent precancerous cervical lesions following treatment in HIV-positive women. The study, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, emphasized the challenges of treatment failure in this group. 3. Greene et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial in Kenya comparing cryotherapy and loop electrosurgical excision procedures (LEEP) for managing high-grade cervical lesions in HIV-positive women. Published in JAMA in 2019, the study assessed the recurrence rates of cervical disease, providing critical insights into the effectiveness of these treatment modalities. 4. Atemnkeng et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2020 to evaluate the impact of antiretroviral therapy (ART) on the detection of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2+) during post-treatment follow-up in HIV-positive women. The findings, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, underscored the role of ART in cervical lesion management. 5. Omange Orang’o et al. investigated the use of visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), Pap smears, and high-risk HPV testing for post-treatment cervical cancer screening in HIV-positive women. Their 2017 study, published in AIDS, highlighted the varying priorities and effectiveness of these screening methods. 6. De Vuyst et al. explored residual disease and HPV persistence after cryotherapy for CIN2/3 in HIV-positive women in Kenya. Published in PLoS One in 2014, the study revealed the limitations of cryotherapy in completely eradicating cervical lesions in this population. 7. A review of follow-up strategies after cervical cancer screening or treatment in the general population identified gaps in evidence regarding optimal follow-up intervals. The analysis compared different screening algorithms and intervals (e.g., every 3, 5, or 10 years) and highlighted the need for more robust data to guide follow-up care. 8. Systematic reviews of primary studies revealed that no research directly compared different follow-up intervals using the same screening algorithm. However, evidence from modeling studies informed recommendations for follow-up intervals after negative or positive screening tests. 9. For women living with HIV, systematic reviews reported the incidence of CIN2-3 after treatment and the sensitivity and specificity of various follow-up tests. These findings informed guidelines for post-treatment cervical cancer screening in this high-risk group. 10. A scoping review of the literature on cervical cancer screening initiation and cessation ages found limited studies comparing outcomes for different age groups. The evidence suggested that starting screening at age 35 versus 30 and ending at age 50 versus older could impact cancer detection rates. 11. Studies on the natural history of CIN lesions demonstrated age-dependent differences in regression, persistence, and progression rates. Younger women (<30 years) showed higher regression rates and lower progression rates compared to older women. 12. Research on HPV prevalence revealed age-specific patterns, with a peak in HPV detection shortly after the onset of sexual activity, followed by a decline in middle-aged women. In some populations, a second peak in older women was observed. 13. Studies on cervical cancer burden in specific regions, such as South Africa and China, highlighted disparities in screening access and HPV prevalence. These findings emphasized the need for targeted interventions to improve screening coverage and outcomes. 14. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses provided robust data on the progression and regression of untreated CIN2 lesions, with younger women showing better outcomes under conservative management. 15. Barriers to cervical cancer screening, particularly among older women, included misconceptions about the necessity of screening, logistical challenges, and discomfort with the procedure. Efforts to address these barriers are critical for improving screening uptake. 16. Studies on patient preferences and provider practices revealed inconsistencies with screening guidelines, such as overscreening in younger women and continued screening in low-risk older women. These findings highlight the need for better adherence to evidence-based recommendations. 17. Equity issues in cervical cancer screening were evident, with disparities in screening access and outcomes based on age, race, and socioeconomic status. Addressing these inequities is essential for improving cervical cancer prevention globally. 18. Research on HPV prevalence and cervical cancer incidence in different populations provided valuable insights into the epidemiology of these conditions, informing public health strategies for prevention and early detection. These findings collectively underscore the importance of evidence-based, population-specific approaches to cervical cancer screening and management, particularly for high-risk groups such as women living with HIV.
